We tested our approach on THE acquired phantom data from the algorithms for mapping elastic modulus Challenge, as well as on in vivo liver THE in 4 healthy volunteers and 14 patients with focal liver lesions, including benign focal nodular hyperplasia, and malignant hepatocellular carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. MF-ElastoNet was successfully adapted to THE with in vivo liver testing. Compared with k-MDEV, the state-of-the-art wave inversion method for THE, Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -0.02 m/s (95% limits of agreement: -0.36 to 0.33 m/s).

papers.title: When Does Looking Closer Pay Off? Simple Foveated ViTs for Fine-Grained Recognition
papers.abstract: Fine-grained recognition benefits from high resolution, but not every image region needs it. We study a foveated Vision Transformer (FoVT) that uses last-block class attention from a 224-pixel glance to select regions for refinement. Fine patches from the 448-pixel image replace the selected coarse cells, and the same backbone classifies the mixed-resolution input. We evaluate FoVT on five benchmarks with two seeds and 26 configurations per dataset. Attention beats random selection on all five benchmarks, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points on the smallest objects. At equal transformer cost, Holm-corrected tests detect no FoVT deficit relative to a port of the official CF-ViT, but no dataset shows a corrected FoVT advantage in both seeds. FoVT requires no feature reuse, distillation loss, or selection schedule. Reusing coarse features shows no significant benefit and costs 1 to 3 points when the reuse module is trained at the head learning rate. Skipping refinement for the most confident 19 to 24 percent of images leaves accuracy unchanged to two decimal places. At the transformer cost of uniform 336-pixel inference, gated FoVT improves accuracy on four benchmarks, with the largest gains on NABirds and FGVC-Aircraft and no significant gain on Stanford Dogs. Foveation primarily saves computation: relative to a uniform 448-pixel model trained with the same auxiliary glance loss, ungated FoVT uses 44 percent fewer transformer operations, with no significant accuracy difference on four benchmarks and a 0.53-point deficit on FGVC-Aircraft. Wall-clock savings are smaller than the reduction in transformer operations.

papers.title: An Autonomous Adaptive Learning System for Robotic Grasping in the Circular Factory
papers.abstract: Linear manufacturing typically operates in highly structured settings with standardized objects, allowing robots to execute pre-programmed motions based on precise models. In contrast, circular manufacturing involves dynamic and less controlled environments, where product components can vary due to appearance and physical changes across different product generations. In this context, uncertainty arises from both the unknown or partially observed states of components (e.g., damaged surfaces, altered shapes) and the unstructured disassembly environment, often characterized by heavy clutter, occlusions, and limited sensing viewpoints. This demands a flexible and adaptable robotic grasping system that can cope with unexpected object changes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an autonomous grasp learning framework designed for highly uncertain and variable conditions. The framework explicitly distinguishes between uncertainty due to noisy or incomplete sensory observations (aleatoric uncertainty) and uncertainty due to limited knowledge and distribution shift (epistemic uncertainty). Moreover, the framework employs an active perception strategy to reduce visual ambiguity: semantic and spatial scene understanding is achieved using vision language models (VLMs), while view planning enables the robot to adjust its viewpoint to improve observability. In addition, the approach leverages large-scale human demonstration data to learn interaction patterns, which are then transferred to robotic end-effectors, enabling robust manipulation in these variable settings. Quantitative validation, including the utility of active vision on disassembled components in practice, is expected to form an important part of future work.

papers.title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
papers.abstract: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

papers.title: Complex chaotic Boltzmann machines as deterministic representations of quantum states
papers.abstract: Neural networks and tensor networks have opened new ways to explore quantum systems by parameterizing families of wave functions through the structure and parameters of a network. Here we extend this perspective to a dynamical representation: we introduce a complex chaotic Boltzmann machine that assigns a deterministic system to a pure quantum state. We extend Suzuki's construction to incorporate both Born probabilities and relative phases. The probabilities set the trajectory velocities in a hypercube, while the phases define a complex field that lifts its Poincare sections. The evolution is determined by the network parameters and initial conditions, without random choices during flights or configuration changes. Our analysis of two qubits and study of three-qubit families show how relations between probabilities organize regular curves, islands, and unstable regions, and how phases distinguish states that share the same Born dynamics. This architecture turns a wave-function parameterization into a geometry of trajectories, providing a tool to explore probabilities, phases, and symmetries together across families of states.

papers.title: Stochastic Extragradient Methods Beyond Lipschitz Continuity
papers.abstract: Stochastic variational inequality problems have received significant attention due to their ability to model large-scale machine learning tasks. Typically, the operators involved are assumed to be globally Lipschitz, with only a handful of works extending beyond the standard setting to the so-called $(L_0,L_1)$-Lipschitz setting. In this work, we propose a novel stochastic past extragradient algorithm for variational inequality problems under a broad regularity assumption that is even less restrictive than $(L_0,L_1)$-Lipschitz continuity and provide convergence guarantees under bounded variance of the stochastic oracle. More precisely, we show a.s. convergence with suitable stepsize schedules and obtain convergence rates in expectation and in probability for fixed horizons. Finally, in numerical simulations we compare our proposed algorithm against standard methods.

papers.title: From Novel Combinations to Informative Absence: Structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice in language learning
papers.abstract: Language learners must infer which novel expressions are grammatically licensed and when continued absence is evidence against them. Our generative theory unites these capacities via counterfactual expression opportunities, decomposing utterance generation into structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice. First, shared predictive continuations recover structural permission for unseen word-construction pairings across 30 artificial grammars (mean AUC 0.945 after 120 sentences). Second, under hierarchical uncertainty, we derive a joint evidence law linking omissions to context diversity and within-context repetition, and an exact finite-sample context-refinement inequality. Thus, observing related expressions calibrates expected use to sharpen negative evidence, and higher expected use can drive steeper posterior declines for stronger-permission candidates (reversing initial order after six omissions in a fixed-rate example). Third, we prove that while raw counts confound semantic availability and form selection, scene-level opportunity observations identify both. Empirically, reanalyzing adult and child artificial-language experiments shows meaning-conditioned restriction; judgments of restricted combinations improve held-out production predictions across 399 participants (+0.036 nats/production). Naturalistic child-directed and child speech (11 families, six corpora) shows pervasive source-level usage clustering beyond lexical, number, and dependency-role controls, grounding hierarchical rate uncertainty. Finally, modeling causative judgments across five languages shows that structural compatibility and calibrated usage probabilities draw on distinct distributional, semantic, and discriminative cues. Together, these findings show how the organization and calibration of communicative opportunities govern the evidential value of linguistic absence.

papers.title: DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.

papers.title: An Asymptotic One-Sample Surrogate for Non-Gaussian ERM with General Convex Regularization
papers.abstract:
We study convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) with non-Gaussian features and nonsmooth penalties through a surrogate driven by a single Gaussian vector. The surrogate preserves the penalty and calibrates its coefficients using the actual joint law of the feature-label model. We prove that this population calibration exists and is unique. We prove a Gaussian approximation for fresh prediction scores when the data satisfy a Poincaré inequality.
  Together with regularity conditions on the losses, this approximation yields agreement between the ERM minimizer and its surrogate in normalized means and prediction variances, as well as formulas for prediction and classification risks. The result covers general uniformly strongly convex penalties and pure Lasso under projection anti-concentration. The core proof relies on a cavity Hamilton-Jacobi argument that compares the main statistics of the two minimizers without differentiating the penalty.

papers.title: Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model
papers.abstract: Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.

papers.title: A Switching Mechanism for Selecting Environment-Adaptive Personalized Gains in Hearing Aids
papers.abstract: Personalized amplification gains for hearing aids have been shown to be preferred over prescriptive gains. Since the preferred settings can vary depending on the background audio environment, this paper presents a switching mechanism or system that automatically selects personalized gains for a current background audio environment. To prevent foreground speech from interfering with background environment analysis, a one-class voice activity detector is designed to identify speech activity from speech mixed with noise. A consistency check is conducted to enable distinguishing foreground speech from background speech, preserving babble as a background environment of interest because hearing aid users often struggle to understand speech in background babble. Sound segments without foreground speech are then analyzed by an online discovery method combining Bayesian change-point detection with a memory of previously encountered environments. This discovery method detects changes, recognizes returning environments, and discovers new ones without a predefined number of environments. Experimental results show that three-seed mean macro-averaged F1 scores of 85.53%-91.98% across eight speech/background-corpus pairs covering 36 background noise types were achieved. Furthermore, the discovery method achieved adjusted Rand indices of 0.91 and 0.96 on two families of test streams. In the same-recording-return condition of audio streams combining speech with four background audio environments often encountered by hearing aid users, the switching mechanism selected the correct personalized gain profile after 105 environment changes, recalled the stored gain profile at every return, and made no switches to an incorrect gain profile.

papers.title: A Cognitive Agentic AI Framework for Interactive Process Analysis and Optimization
papers.abstract: Complex multivariable process analysis and optimization require coordinated access to simulation, structured data, machine learning (ML), optimization, and scientific literature, often across disconnected software tools. We present a Cognitive Agentic AI Framework (CAAF) that enables interactive, iterative process investigation through natural-language prompts within an established flowsheet. Following harness-engineering principles, CAAF assigns task interpretation, planning, knowledge synthesis, and context management to a large language model while delegating numerical calculations to specialized tools. Dedicated providers connect databases, scientific-document retrieval, ML-assisted Bayesian optimization (BO), and COCO process simulation. The framework is demonstrated on methyl acetate production. Guided by successive prompts, an engineer explored multivariable relationships, conducted 4,000 BO iterations to maximize carbon conversion yield (C-Yield) and minimize specific energy cost (C-SEC), refined operating bounds, and verified selected candidates through process simulation. Re-simulation of 16 candidates within the restricted domain showed close agreement with ML predictions, with a mean absolute C-Yield error of 0.0085 (0.85 percentage points). The highest BO-derived C-Yield, verified by COCO, was 0.921 versus approximately 0.81 in the initial dataset, an improvement of about 11 percentage points. CAAF also detects and reports non-converged simulations, excludes invalid outputs, and continues subsequent evaluations. The results demonstrate how human-guided agentic coordination can combine engineering tools for iterative analysis and optimization with rigorous simulation-based verification under a fixed process topology.

papers.title: Beyond Math, Code, and Logic: Do Reasoning Models Transfer to Scientific Argumentation?
papers.abstract: Scientific discourse depends on argumentative reasoning: identifying claims, evaluating evidence, and constructing coherent responses. While recent advances in reasoning-capable language models have demonstrated strong performance on mathematical, coding, and logical benchmarks, their ability to engage in scientific argumentation remains unclear. We present the first systematic evaluation of language models across seven tasks spanning argument mining, rebuttal generation, and discourse-level reasoning using research papers, peer reviews, and grant proposals. Our study reveals that even frontier models with strong general reasoning skills struggle with domain-specific argumentative tasks, highlighting a fundamental capability gap. To address this, we introduce a training framework that explicitly scaffolds the argumentative reasoning process in language models, substantially improving their competence in scientific discourse. The resulting compact models approach or exceed the performance of much larger proprietary systems and generalize to unseen conversational settings, demonstrating reasoning transfer beyond task-specific supervision. These findings underscore that effective scientific argumentation is not an emergent property of scale, but requires explicit reasoning-aware training, and they point toward practical pathways for building AI systems that can contribute meaningfully to scientific discourse.

papers.title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
papers.abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.

papers.title: PAWS: A Parametric Model of Canine Pose and Shape
papers.abstract:
We introduce PAWS, a parametric model of canine shape and pose, learned from 3D scans of real dogs. Capturing the full diversity of dogs is challenging, as different breeds vary in size, proportion, and body shape. To capture this range, we scanned 31 dogs across multiple breeds and sizes performing a range of natural movements. From this dataset, we build a parametric model that combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space learned from the 3D scans. Unlike previous models, our model is learned from real dogs in varying poses, allowing for realistic modelling of canine pose and shape.
  We demonstrate that building on PAWS provides a robust framework for downstream tasks, such as surface reconstruction and image regression. In particular, we show that a limited number of anatomically valid degrees of freedom is sufficient to accurately estimate dog pose and shape.

papers.title: VeilGS: Solving Darkness as a Veil of 2D Basis Maps over Retinex 3DGS
papers.abstract: In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.

papers.title: Solving the pre-image problem in kernel PCA: The reproducing property is all you need
papers.abstract: Kernel PCA extends PCA to nonlinear dimensionality reduction by implicitly mapping data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via the kernel trick, with applications ranging from image denoising to out-of-distribution detection. While its projection map is well understood, appropriately defining the associated reconstruction map is a longstanding challenge since projecting back from the RKHS to the input space is non-trivial. This is known as the pre-image problem. Existing approaches have tackled this problem by either relying on nonlinear optimization, which is prone to numerical instabilities and sensitive to initialization, or by solving a separate supervised learning problem, incurring additional computational overhead. Furthermore, although the projection map of kernel PCA reduces to that of standard PCA when a linear kernel is used, most of these approaches are not guaranteed to recover PCA's reconstruction map in this case, a consistency property that one would naturally expect to hold. In this paper, we leverage the reproducing property of the RKHS to derive a reconstruction map for kernel PCA that is provably consistent. Our derivations rely on the mild assumption that the RKHS either contains linear functions or the kernel is universal, which holds for standard kernels. We further extend the method to the random Fourier features (RFFs) approximation of kernel PCA by introducing a corresponding notion of RFF reproducing property. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs comparably with state-of-the-art methods across kernel choices, while remaining more computationally efficient and maintaining consistent performance in settings where these baseline methods drastically fail.

papers.title: Efficient inference for fairness-constrained sequential decision policies
papers.abstract: Adaptive decision systems in education and health choose interventions sequentially and are often required not to leave a protected group too far behind. We study the fairness-constrained optimal value: the largest population value attainable by a policy in a smooth parametric class subject to constraints that are smooth functions of group specific counterfactual functionals, such as value gaps, floors, max-min welfare and budgets. For multi-stage, non-Markov data under sequential ignorability, a sensitivity analysis of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker system shows that this value is pathwise differentiable, with efficient influence function equal to the Lagrangian combination of the influence functions of the group values. The same analysis gives the influence functions of the optimal policy, the multiplier and the group values it delivers. A cross-fitted doubly robust estimator is efficient despite its data-dependent feasible set and yields confidence intervals for the constrained value and the price of fairness. When the constraint binds, any plug-in fair policy violates the population constraint, by a margin that vanishes as the sample grows, with probability tending to one half; tightening the estimated constraint by a one sided confidence margin certifies fairness at a small cost in value. Exact checks, simulations and a synthetic case study illustrate the theory.

papers.title: When Are Images Needed in Multimodal Machine Translation? Text-Only Routing for On-Demand Visual Context
papers.abstract: Image-guided multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to resolve translation-relevant uncertainty. However, prevailing systems either process images unconditionally or apply gating only after visual encoding, leaving redundant visual computation unavoidable. To mitigate this computational overhead, routing decisions must rely on a pre-visual source signal. Crucially, surface-level ambiguity does not equate to visual dependence, as intra-sentence textual context often suffices for disambiguation. We therefore formulate visual invocation as source-text sufficiency prediction: determining exclusively from the source text whether translation-relevant uncertainty remains unresolved. To support this formulation, we construct a visual-dependency dataset with three fine-grained labels (no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed) and verify discriminative visual evidence for vision_needed instances. We further propose PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic text-only router that selects between text-only and multimodal branches before computing visual features. Experiments on English-to-Chinese MMT demonstrate that PreVIR achieves a favorable COMET-budget trade-off relative to strong routing baselines. At its default operating point, it substantially reduces visual calls while maintaining translation quality comparable to always-on multimodal inference. Label-wise and case analyses show that this trade-off stems from distinguishing genuine visual dependency from contextually resolved ambiguity.

papers.title: Beyond the Ground State: Assessing the Machine-Learned Skala Functional in ΔSCF Calculations of Molecular Excitation Energies
papers.abstract: We assess the transferability of the machine-learned Skala exchange-correlation (XC) functional beyond ground-state energetics using molecular vertical excitation energies and singlet-triplet gaps calculated with the $Δ$-self-consistent-field ($Δ$SCF) approach. We compare Skala with PBE, r$^2$SCAN, and PBE0 on subsets covering small-molecule excitations (QUEST1), inverted singlet-triplet gaps (ST-gap), and intramolecular charge-transfer excitations (QUEST6). Both spin-unrestricted Kohn-Sham (UKS) and restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham (ROKS) formalisms are considered. On QUEST1, Skala achieves the lowest mean absolute errors (MAEs) for singlet and triplet excitation energies with both formalisms, although PBE0 and r$^2$SCAN provide more accurate singlet-triplet gaps through error cancellation. For ST-gap, Skala yields the lowest gap MAEs with both UKS and ROKS. Evaluating the mixed-spin and triplet energy components on the same orbitals optimized for the ROKS open-shell singlet yields negative splittings for seven of eight ST-gap molecules with Skala. Separate triplet optimization increases the gaps, but six remain negative. All three conventional functionals give positive common-orbital splittings and optimized gaps for all eight molecules. For QUEST6, treated with UKS only, Skala yields more accurate singlet excitation energies than PBE and r$^2$SCAN but remains less accurate than PBE0. Across QUEST1 and ST-gap, Skala yields lower MAEs with UKS than ROKS. Overall, these results support Skala's transferability to molecular excited states while highlighting its dependence on the excitation class and open-shell treatment.

papers.title: Stall-Triggered Newton-Krylov-Assisted DIIS and Its Machine-Learning-Accelerated Variant for CCSD Convergence
papers.abstract: The iterative solution of the non-linear amplitude equations of coupled-cluster singles doubles (CCSD) theory can encounter convergence instabilities, asymptotic convergence or outright divergence. Direct Inversion in the Iterative Subspace (DIIS) is a widely used extrapolation technique but can also exhibit slow or oscillatory convergence in challenging regimes. In this work, we introduce a robust hybrid solver: Stall-Triggered Newton-Krylov Assisted DIIS (${}{\mathrm{st}}$NK-DIIS) alongside its machine-learning accelerated variant ${}{\mathrm{st}}$NK$^{\mathrm{ML}}$-DIIS which leverages the robust convergence of Newton-Krylov (NK) while avoiding the high computational cost of Krylov iterations. In our methods, DIIS remains the default accelerator and a matrix-free NK procedure is activated when sustained stagnation or divergence is detected with each NK step verified using the non-linear residual before acceptance. To alleviate the cost of Krylov iterations the ${}{\mathrm{st}}$NK$^{\mathrm{ML}}$-DIIS uses a gated recurrent unit (GRU) to predict a scalar logarithmic step-size ratio along the approximately computed Newton direction. When the ML-predicted step fails residual-based verification, the method falls back to a grid-based NK line search. Using CCSD as the underlying electronic-structure theory, we evaluate these methods against conventional DIIS and pure NK for stretched molecules exhibiting convergence difficulties in terms of residual convergence, iteration counts, and wall-time performance. These protocols may be generalizable to other non-linear equation solvers as well, as the ML model learns the convergence pattern of the variables and does not require system-specific knowledge such as atom identities or molecular orbital properties. This allows transferability across atom-type, bonding character and basis-sets.

papers.title: Geometrically Constrained Learning II: Agnostic Proper Learning of Lipschitz Functions
papers.abstract:
We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given random Gaussian examples labeled by a $λ$-Lipschitz function, $λ\ge 1$, the learner returns a function $h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that is globally $λ$-Lipschitz and has loss (absolute or squared) at most $\varepsilon$. The sample complexity, running time, and representation size are \[
  (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(λ/\varepsilon)}. \] The learning algorithm can be made \emph{agnostic}, given a known bound on the variance of the label marginal distribution. Some known control of label scale is information-theoretically necessary. For arbitrary labels with variance at most $V^2 \ge 1$, the complexity is \[
  (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(Vλ/\varepsilon)}, \] and the error is $\mathsf{opt} + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}$ is the minimal error among Lipschitz approximators.
  Our approach combines $L_1$ polynomial regression under a convex gradient constraint with local correction of the Lipschitz property. The learner finds a polynomial that, after smoothing and clipping its range, is very close to a canonical Lipschitz correction of itself, the lower Lipschitz envelope. Our local corrector modifies the lower envelope by replacing distances to sublevel sets with a Gaussian sampling proxy, allowing the construction to be locally and stably estimated from samples.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process
papers.abstract: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.

papers.title: Comparative Performance of Machine Learning Architectures for Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Chemical Processes
papers.abstract: Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) is crucial for both maintenance and control in chemical industries, where early fault detection can prevent costly failures and optimize operations. This is particularly critical in pilot units like those at IFP Energies Nouvelles (IFPEN), which operate under short-term experimental conditions with frequently varying operational parameters. This study conducts an extensive benchmarking analysis using the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP), a widely used simulated chemical process dataset, to evaluate multiple approaches for fault detection and diagnosis, featuring numerous continuous operations with different sensors and faults. Several methods were implemented and compared including Multi Scale PCA (MS-PCA), AutoEncoder, Ensemble Learning, and LSTM models for fault detection, alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and BLSTM (Bidirectional LSTM) for fault diagnosis. Our results demonstrate that Ensemble Learning achieves detection rates ranging from 80% to 100% across various fault scenarios. For the fault diagnosis task, BLSTM achieved a diagnosis accuracy of 98.76%. The study reveals that ensemble-based approaches consistently outperform individual models in handling the complex, multivariate nature of chemical process data, due to its robustness in combining multiple perspectives, comprehensive data capture, and localized detection capabilities. Furthermore, the superior performance of the BLSTM is due to its ability to capture both past and future temporal dependencies in the sequential data, particularly important in chemical processes where fault patterns may manifest with complex temporal relationships. This research contributes to the field of Fault Detection and Diagnosis by providing empirical evidence for the effectiveness of ensemble methods and Bidirectional LSTMs in order to address industrial FDD applications on chemical processes.

papers.title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.

papers.title: CanopyFormer: Attention-Guided SegFormer for Explainable Forest Cover Segmentation
papers.abstract: In transformer segmentation models, attention is usually visualized after training rather than supervised. Although attention supervision has been explored for natural images and driving scenes, aerial forest segmentation typically uses attention only as an architectural component and evaluates interpretability qualitatively. We present CanopyFormer, an attention-guided SegFormer-B0 that uses an Attention Consistency Loss to align attention with the ground-truth forest mask, encouraging attention to focus on canopy regions. Since SegFormer uses spatial-reduction attention, we adapt Gradient-weighted Attention Rollout by restricting it to the final encoder stage, where the attention matrix is square. We introduce Average Attention-Mask Overlap (AAMO) to measure attention alignment and incorporate a deletion test to evaluate faithfulness. On 5108 images, our method increases AAMO from 0.0334 to 0.7476, approximately 22 times the vanilla SegFormer-B0 result, with a modest decrease in Dice score from 0.8743 to 0.8577. The deletion test reveals that improved alignment does not necessarily translate into improved faithfulness: removing the most-attended 25% of patches reduces the forest score by 12.1%, compared with 33.0% when removing random patches. Attention supervision introduces no additional inference cost, although double backpropagation makes each training step 2.6 to 2.8 times slower. The attention alignment improvement also generalizes to a second dataset, LoveDA. Additionally, a Boundary Refinement Module provides no consistent Dice improvement and reduces AAMO, while mean squared error substantially outperforms Kullback-Leibler divergence as the attention loss.

papers.title: Closed-loop policy optimisation for cylinder wake control via differentiable simulation
papers.abstract: Suppressing vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder is a classical problem in active flow control.Model-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) learns such policies by interacting with the flow without differentiating its dynamics, which typically requires a large interaction budget. This study optimises closed-loop policies by differentiable simulation: control-loss gradients propagate through the simulated flow to the policy parameters, which are updated by reverse-mode automatic differentiation. The policy maps local velocity measurements to a jet amplitude imposed through differentiable synthetic-jet boundary conditions. In a two-dimensional confined cylinder wake at Rey=100, eight policy updates (about 78 shedding periods of forward simulation) give approximately 8% drag reduction and 99.6% suppression of lift fluctuations, the drag level being comparable to reported DRL results. Suppression is sustained by feedback: a mean-matched constant jet does not maintain it, whereas the same policy responds similarly at three activation phases and recovers after upstream disturbances. A velocity-deviation reward alone retains strong suppression, and observations of two instantaneous velocity components at one near-wake or surface location reach about 99.8% suppression, whereas a single surface pressure leaves residual oscillations. Together with related DRL results, this suggests that reward and observation requirements here are set by policy optimisation and flow physics.

papers.title: Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for Estimating Visitation to Natural Spaces in the UK
papers.abstract: Natural spaces support health and well-being, but increasing recreational use can put pressure on ecologically sensitive sites. Understanding when, where and why people visit is important for planning, site management and evaluating interventions. Building on work by the Office for National Statistics, we developed statistical and machine learning models to predict visitor numbers at points located in natural spaces. We trained on automated people counter data across a range of green and blue spaces in England and Wales and tested the models' ability to generalise to unseen counter locations. Our models offer a scalable approach for predicting visitor numbers in natural spaces, reducing reliance on surveys and physical counters.

papers.title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
papers.abstract: Semiparametric models provide a broad framework for statistical inference, yet efficient estimation typically relies on influence function correction tailored to each estimand and on nuisance estimation repeated for every sample. We show that a single pretrained Transformer can deliver efficient estimation and valid inference for a family of estimands in one forward pass, without deriving efficient influence functions or estimating nuisance functions. Pretrained on simulated data with the true parameter as the only label, the Transformer learns the posterior mean and covariance of the queried estimand and hence returns an estimate and a Wald-type confidence region. Theoretically, we prove that, for locally flat pretraining priors of slowly growing complexity, the posterior mean is efficient for every queried estimand. The Transformer inherits this efficiency with asymptotically exact coverage, in probability over evaluation populations and queries, even under distribution shift. We also reveal that the guarantee places much higher demands on pretraining when the data-generating distribution is fixed, as in classical frequentist inference. Experiments on causal inference, partial linear regression, and survival analysis show that the pretrained model generally achieves the lowest estimation error among competing methods, with nearly nominal coverage, at a computational cost of only about 0.02 seconds per dataset.

papers.title: SMSD: A Semantic Misinformation Spreader Detection Approach
papers.abstract: Misinformation spreaders on social media significantly amplify false narratives, making early detection critical to mitigate their spread. Existing approaches often overlook evolving user behavior, introduce semantic noise by ignoring user stance, and fail to handle newly emerging users effectively. To address these limitations, we propose a \underline{S}emantic \underline{M}isinformation \underline{S}preader \underline{D}etection approach (SMSD) that models misinformation propagation as a temporal, user-centric, and behavior-driven learning problem. SMSD adopts a multimodal architecture that incorporates three categories of features: user-level, network-level, and conversation propagation. A stance-aware labeling strategy is also introduced to differentiate supportive, opposing, questioning, and neutral users towards misinformation claims. Additionally, a monthly quantile analysis is introduced to simulate realistic, evolving user participation. Initial experimental results on the FibVid COVID-19 benchmark dataset demonstrate that SMSD improves recall by 45.0\%, F1 by 49.5\%, and MCC by 74.6\% under stance-aware labeling and by 17.7\%, 7.4\%, and 11.4\%, respectively, under threshold-based labeling. It consistently outperforms all baselines in both settings.

papers.title: Hierarchical Agentic Mid-Band Agility for Reliable Low-Latency Space-Air-Ground Integrated V2X Networks
papers.abstract: Upper-mid-band spectrum offers bandwidth opportunities for the integrated networks of ground vehicles, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites to support 6G wide-area vehicle-to-everything (V2X) connectivity. However, V2X services' latency and reliability are sensitive to the mid-band selection due to frequency-dependent propagation and rain attenuation. This paper investigates environment-aware spectrum agility over candidate frequency range 3 (FR3) bands within 7.125-24.25 GHz, jointly with end-to-end (E2E) multi-path traffic splitting and transmit power control. Each data packet is partitioned into non-overlapping subflows over direct and UAV-assisted paths, with failed sky-link subflows selectively retransmitted subject to retransmission and freshness constraints. We formulate latency- and reliability-oriented problems, followed by a unified sequential optimization problem incorporating band-switching costs and average quality-of-service (QoS) violation budgets. To coordinate optimization decisions across heterogeneous timescales, we develop an agentic AI-assisted hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning (AA-HMARL) framework. A high-level agentic supervisor integrates recurrent memory, analytical evaluation of candidate bands, and event-triggered replanning to coordinate slow environmental adaptation with fast channel and retransmission dynamics, while distributed ground vehicles and UAV agents optimize data splitting and power using constrained MAPPO. Simulation results demonstrate an adjustable reliability-latency trade-off. Particularly, AA-HMARL reduces the mean E2E completion latency and the mean number of retransmission rounds among successfully delivered updates by 17.8-25.5% and 57.6-61.5%, respectively, and reduces the mean age of information (AoI) by 12.7-14.6% relative to fixed-band MAPPO across two traffic types.

papers.title: Beyond Sample Hardness: Adaptive Data Selection through Learning Dynamics
papers.abstract: Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs. However, most existing methods often rely heavily on sample hardness, which may overlook differences in sample learning dynamics and lead to suboptimal sample selection. In this paper, we propose LeDAS, an end-to-end Learning Dynamics-Aware Selection framework for dynamic data selection, which jointly characterizes sample importance through hardness, learning progress, and deterioration, enabling adaptive sample prioritization throughout training with marginal additional computational overhead. Specifically, we track per-sample loss dynamics using exponential moving averages (EMA) to obtain three complementary signals that capture current learning difficulty, ongoing learning improvements, and potential degradation. To accommodate evolving training dynamics, we introduce Adaptive Metric Fusion, a contextual bandit-based mechanism that dynamically adjusts the relative importance of these signals based on training feedback. Furthermore, a bounded staleness compensation mechanism accounts for historical selection patterns by increasing the selection priority of samples that have not been selected for extended periods. Extensive experiments across diverse vision and language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of LeDAS. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, LeDAS consistently achieves superior performance, matching or surpassing full-dataset training at a 50\% selection ratio on ImageNet-1K and in LLM supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, its modular and task-agnostic design enables the integration of complementary selection signals, demonstrating strong robustness to noisy and corrupted datasets.

papers.title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning
papers.abstract: Generative models transform simple random inputs into samples that resemble observed data. For a finite training set, a central question is how its geometry shapes the terminal dynamics and the probabilities assigned to individual samples. We address this question for flow matching with linear interpolation between independent Gaussian and empirical samples. The squared distance to the training set generates explicit paths contracting exponentially toward the nearest sample. We prove that exact trajectories restarted at prescribed late-time states approximate these paths uniformly over all elapsed times and compact sets of starting states away from Voronoi interfaces, with an error exponentially small in the inverse squared restart noise scale. The initial mass near interfaces controls the quadratic Wasserstein error between the exact and reference laws. For Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restart laws, this gives a square-root rate in the restart noise scale, uniform over time, which a two-site example shows to be sharp in general. At ties, the Clarke subdifferential characterizes the graphical limit of the rescaled velocity field. This geometry motivates two learning methods: fitting the distance potential with value and gradient supervision, and fitting velocities along explicit contraction paths. A transport estimate separates initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation. MNIST experiments illustrate the distinct roles of support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity. These results connect flow matching and score-based diffusion through a common limiting geometry and show how asymptotic analysis can inform the design and evaluation of generative models.

papers.title: Auditing Post-Training Unlearning in Diffusion Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). DLMs generate text through iterative denoising, exposing partially masked states whose internal representations change throughout the generation process. This raises a DLM-specific question: can selective forgetting improve by identifying forget-data-associated features and adapting their suppression across denoising stages? We conduct a controlled investigation of this question in LLaDA-8B-Instruct. To evaluate the unlearning of knowledge plausibly encoded during pre-training, we use WMDP as our forget-domain benchmark. Using top-k sparse autoencoders and denoising-state replay, we compare static and stage-adaptive feature suppression. We find substantial shifts in forget-data-associated features across denoising stages, but tracking these dynamics alone does not reliably improve the forget-retain trade-off at the evaluated operating points. Together, our study provides an initial empirical foundation for developing and evaluating machine unlearning as a post-training privacy mechanism in DLMs.

papers.title: Trust What Repeats: Capped World-Model Policy Gradients for Humanoid Motion Tracking
papers.abstract: Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker for the Unitree G1, the $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved along the model's gradient, the simulator returns 94% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is below the batch median, 48% between 3 and 10 times the median, and 1% above 30 times; the part of a gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout's action-gradient norm at 10 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return. Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.953 to 0.967 and the lowest $1\%$ of test clips from 0.65 to 0.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 15--18 to 7--10, and reaches the baseline's final return in 40% of the baseline's iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.935 against 0.906.

papers.title: Cyclic perturbations encode memories in trained neural networks without loss of performance
papers.abstract: Many disordered materials exhibit a remarkable form of memory: they retain information about the history of cyclic perturbations. Whether this phenomenon also occurs in artificial neural networks, whose mathematical structure and dynamics share many similarities with disordered physical systems, is unknown. Here we show that cyclically perturbing a trained, overparameterized deep neural network encodes information in the structure of the weights that can subsequently be retrieved, thus retaining memory of the perturbation history. During each write cycle, all weights are displaced, after which the network relaxes through gradient descent. Repeated cycles organise the neural network into a state that is reversible for perturbations up to the write amplitude, allowing the encoded value to be read from the onset of irreversible weight motion. Multiple memories can also be encoded, although under deterministic writing only the largest persists at long times. Inspired by cyclically sheared suspensions, we introduce a novel noisy-write protocol that preserves all encoded memories at long times. Remarkably, neither deterministic nor noisy memory writing measurably affects the network's performance on unseen data from its original learning task. Our results establish cyclic memory as a phenomenon shared by disordered physical systems and deep neural networks, and show that networks can exploit as yet unexplored memory capabilities without compromising their original function.

papers.title: Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Subchunk Rollouts in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.

papers.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
papers.abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

papers.title: Seeing Is Not Steering: Where Verifiable Reasoning Can Enter an End-to-End Driving Planner
papers.abstract: Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner's facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner's facts remains unresolved.

papers.title: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization benchmark problems from mixed Hamming packings
papers.abstract: Benchmarking exact solvers and noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) requires small yet challenging instances, preferably coming from actual applications. We propose such a benchmark set derived from mixed Hamming packing, a hard problem in coding theory. Starting from its mixed-integer linear programming formulation, we provide a generator for the equivalent QUBO models and study 133 instances whose optima are certified by that formulation. In the feature space of the MQLib library, we position a broad range of existing quantum-oriented benchmarks relative to the classical ones: they lie along a narrow, sparse border of the region covered by MQLib, whereas our instances form a coherent family in a region that both collections leave almost empty. Classical heuristics and a simulated bifurcation machine find the optimum of most instances quickly, in several cases sooner than an exact mixed-integer solver first encounters it, suggesting heuristic warm starts for exact solvers; for an exact QUBO solver, in turn, it appears challenging to prove optimality. In Ising form, the instances are densely connected antiferromagnets whose large local fields are almost exactly balanced by the couplings, so that the decision on each variable rests on a small remainder. This makes them hard to embed and to represent accurately on current quantum annealers, in line with our D-Wave experiments.

papers.title: Learning Inside Types: Epistemic Typestates for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Type disciplines make programs safe by construction: components checked against each other's types compose into programs that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Types suit reinforcement learning: a type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy a learner produces. We introduce epistemic typestates, a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning. An agent's type is a protocol whose states record its beliefs, the worlds it cannot rule out from its own observations and actions, and permits only actions that are safe in every world of the belief, whatever the others do within their public types. Agents learn inside their types, which are built and checked one agent at a time and run without communication. We prove type soundness and team safety, give a synthesis that is sound and complete, build types from guards when worlds are infinite, and show that shields are a special case. All proofs are mechanised in Rocq. On nine benchmarks, no typed learner causes a safety violation, and task performance does not differ significantly from that of two recent multi-agent shielding methods. Where a contract-based method fails at five and ten agents, types for ten agents are built in under a second. In the two continuous benchmarks, Lagrangian learners cause thousands of violations in every training run.

papers.title: Sketch2TikZ: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning for Converting Hand-Drawn Sketches to Executable TikZ
papers.abstract: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.

papers.title: Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective
papers.abstract: There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint changes in reward and state entropy provide consistency evidence. States thus provide a quantitative description of how post-training organises agent behaviour.

papers.title: Do Econophysics-Inspired Inputs Improve Neural Covariance Forecasting? A Leakage-Free Walk-Forward Study of Intraday DJIA Data
papers.abstract: Tools from econophysics, including Random Matrix Theory (RMT), Tsallis q-Gaussian tails, Hawkes self-excitation and diffusion-inspired regularization, are often proposed as ingredients for financial risk models, but their incremental value over strong contemporary benchmarks remains unclear. We introduce a Physics-Inspired Neural Covariance (PINC) framework for one-day-ahead covariance forecasting using 1-minute data from the 29 Dow Jones Industrial Average constituents over 545 trading days. The model incorporates RMT-cleaned correlations, Tsallis tail indices and Hawkes intensities as inputs and optionally includes a Fokker-Planck-inspired regularization term selected strictly on validation data. Evaluation is performed through a nested walk-forward design with 11 folds, 231 out-of-sample trading days and multiple random seeds, with explicit leakage controls and reproducibility tests. Neural models outperform static covariance estimators such as sample, Ledoit-Wolf, RMT and EVT-based estimators, but show no statistically significant improvement over HAR-RV or LSTM benchmarks. Validation consistently rejects the physics-inspired regularizer, and ablation studies find no measurable contribution from the RMT, Tsallis or Hawkes features. Portfolio experiments show no statistically significant Sharpe ratio improvement after transaction costs. These results suggest that, for this dataset and forecasting horizon, econophysics-inspired components do not provide measurable benefits beyond strong financial forecasting benchmarks.

papers.title: Circular Predictive Coding Unlocks Effective Depth
papers.abstract: Predictive coding networks perform credit assignment through an energy minimization process. Despite their ability to train models with arbitrary network topologies, they have mostly been used to train feedforward architectures to match the performance of backpropagation. However, they fail to do so when the models become too deep, because error signals become unstable or vanish as they travel through many layers. We address this limitation with circular networks, which get their depth directly from the energy minimization, rather than from stacking layers. Formally, we prove that convergence to an equilibrium of the energy functional of a circular predictive coding network approximates the fixed-point iteration process of a deep equilibrium model, showing that circularity alone suffices to unlock effective depth. Empirically, we show that circular models (i) outperform other predictive coding models of the same size on image classification tasks, matching the accuracy of state-of-the-art predictive coding ResNets and VGG networks despite having substantially fewer parameters; (ii) solve constraint satisfaction problems that require many steps of iterative reasoning, a task not feasible with feedforward models at all, reaching 99.3% test accuracy on Sudoku-hard via nested energy minimization loops; and (iii) scale to autoregressive language modeling by training a circular transformer on TinyStories and WikiText-103, before out of reach for predictive coding models. These results have direct implications for physical neural networks, where computational depth can be traded for recursion on a fixed-size circuit.

papers.title: Quantum-Informed Regularized Poisson Learning for Graph-Based Semi-Supervised Classification
papers.abstract: We introduce IPQSSL, a quantum-informed regularized Poisson framework for graph-based semi-supervised classification under scarce labels. Local graph feature contexts are QR factorized, lifted to unitary encodings, and processed by a shared variational circuit whose measurements yield node wise diagonal weights that stabilize a symmetrized Poisson system. We establish positive definiteness of the symmetrized, regularized operator under explicit spectral conditions and derive a Hermitian, block encoding compatible formulation that separates the classical NISQ oriented implementation from a future fault-tolerant pathway. Across seven benchmarks spanning tabular data and a citation network, the effect of regularization is dataset- and budget-dependent: IPQSSL improves over the Poisson baselines on Iris and Wine at all but the single-label budget, reaching 0.946 accuracy on Iris at ten labels per class and at every budget on German Credit, where, however, all methods remain below the majority class rate. Original Poisson remains preferable on Breast Cancer, Heart Disease, Optdigits, and Cora, with the deficit narrowing as the label budget grows on the two largest graphs. Ablations attribute the gains to diagonal stabilization rather than variational training. The result is a resource transparent bridge between Poisson graph learning and quantum linear algebra, with an explicit empirical delineation of when diagonal regularization helps.

papers.title: Tasklets: A Unit-Test Benchmark for Language Model Architectures
papers.abstract: We introduce Tasklets, a benchmark of small synthetic tasks for evaluating the computational capabilities of language model sequence-mixing layers. These tasks probe foundational capabilities such as recall, sequence manipulation, and state tracking. Such tasks are widely used in architecture research, but differences in task selection, formulation, and evaluation make comparisons across studies difficult. Tasklets brings these tasks together, organizing them by the capabilities they test and providing a shared setup for evaluating how different architectural layer types learn fundamental computations. We compare a broad range of layer types through controlled experiments with small models. Our task implementations and evaluation code support reproducible, low-cost testing of new architectural proposals: https://github.com/zaydzuhri/flame/tree/tasklets.

papers.title: Adapting AI Weather Foundation Models to a Changing Climate
papers.abstract: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. We develop an online adaptation framework that exploits two complementary error structures: geographically persistent biases and flow-dependent errors that vary with the atmospheric state. Analysis of Aurora-1.3B reveals strongly concentrated forecast-loss sensitivity in its decoder, motivating flow-dependent corrections within fixed low-dimensional sensitivity subspaces. A residual memory tracks persistent errors remaining after this correction, while a variable-wise online gate controls the contribution of the persistent component. We evaluate Aurora-1.3B using ERA5 from 1959--1968 for offline initialization and a strictly chronological 1969--2022 stream for online evaluation, with updates restricted to previously available verification targets. For 2-metre temperature, distributional departure from the historical reference, measured directly from ERA5, is associated with larger frozen-model errors and greater adaptation gains, while the adapted model maintains more stable skill across evaluation periods. Across 69 output fields and five lead times from 6 to 72 hours, our method reduces MSE and MAE by 6.90\% and 6.45\%, respectively, relative to $δ$-Adapter, the strongest of six online adaptation baselines.

papers.title: Synthesizing Expressive Human-Object Interactions via Test-time Latent Adaptation
papers.abstract: When interacting with objects of unknown physical properties, humans sometimes probe, over-exert, stagger, and adjust through iterative adaptation instead of succeeding immediately. We argue that this process is an expressive but largely overlooked aspect of human-object interaction in motion synthesis. Both kinematic data-driven methods and physics-based controllers tend to produce flawlessly executed motions: the former lack sufficient data for learning fine-grained adaptation, while the latter use reinforcement learning (RL) and privileged object dynamics to learn robust, deterministic behaviors. We propose ExpHOI (Expressive Human-Object Interaction), a test-time latent adaptation framework built on an RL-trained physics-based control policy. During policy training, we encode diverse object dynamics contexts into a structured latent space. At test time, Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) iteratively optimizes the latent code for an object with unknown physical properties. Temporary mismatches between this code and the true object dynamics produce an expressive progression from tentative, error-prone trials to proficient interaction. Adaptation behaviors inevitably come with occasional failures, so a high-level planner is introduced to handle failed cases to maintain full, consistent animations. We demonstrate our framework's effectiveness on a large-object transportation task, where such adaptation is especially pronounced. To train our framework, we introduce a mass-diverse object dataset with rich physical-property annotations. Across carrying and push-pull, our method pairs over 90% success with markedly higher posture diversity, and is rated the most lifelike in our user study on animation liveliness.

papers.title: ReCoFlow-MRI: Few-Step Conditional Flow Matching for GNL-Induced Nonlinear MRI Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Objective: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction is challenging in the presence of gradient nonlinearity (GNL). GNL-induced nonlinear spatial encoding causes geometric distortions that compromise image-guided radiotherapy. Diffusion models require extensive sampling and rarely account for GNL. Flow matching shortens sampling, but velocity matching does not directly minimize the reconstruction error. We propose ReCoFlow-MRI, a conditional flow-matching framework for few-step GNL-corrected reconstruction. Methods: The calibrated GNL displacement field is integrated into the nonlinear encoding model to construct a distortion-corrected zero-filled image, which conditions a velocity field learned along a linear path from Gaussian noise to fully sampled images. The pretrained network is fine-tuned with a pixel-supervised endpoint loss on its five-step reconstruction. Results: On simulated fastMRI brain data, five-step ReCoFlow-MRI achieved the highest PSNR and SSIM among compared methods, including 128-step diffusion sampling. On MRI-Linac phantom and volunteer data, it achieved effective reconstruction and reduced the maximal geometric error from 24.95 to 2.12 mm, with 98.39% of the 3718 fiducial markers below 1 mm. Conclusion: ReCoFlow-MRI jointly addresses undersampling artifacts and geometric distortions within a few-step generative reconstruction. Significance: It provides a potential solution for fast and geometrically accurate imaging in image-guided radiotherapy.

papers.title: Block Search Conditioned on Features for Sequential Quantum Data Encoding
papers.abstract: Sequential quantum data encoding is addressed through the joint selection of input features and encoding blocks within a fixed quantum register. At each step, a new feature, a block of operations, its placement, and its rotation weights are selected together from training data, extending the incremental construction of Q-FLAIR. With direct-loss selection (RAW), nine to twelve features were retained in four qubits across five new Bars and Stripes datasets. Under the same final calibration, mean changes relative to the calibrated Q-FLAIR reference were +5.53 percentage points in balanced accuracy, -15.83% in binary cross-entropy (BCE), and +7.79% in area under the ROC curve (AUC). The prespecified success criterion was met in four of five datasets and for the mean paired differences. These results were obtained by comparing complete procedures under a common cap of 32 operations.
